---
title: "Toolchain step: scripts and assets"
---

The chapter on the starter project left one folder empty on purpose, and this
part filled it with your first stand-alone `.svg`. Now your program learns to
point at that file, and you find out what `npm run build` really produces.

## A picture your program picks {#sec-toolchain-assets-experiment}

Create a new app `assets-tour` from our template inside `coursework/`. Save
this drawing as `assets/badge.svg`:

```html
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 100 100" width="100" height="100" role="img" aria-label="A gold badge">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="45" fill="gold" stroke="darkorange" stroke-width="6" />
  <text x="50" y="62" font-size="34" text-anchor="middle" fill="darkorange">3.6</text>
</svg>
```

Put an empty image below the heading in `index.html`:

```html
<img id="badgeImage" alt="A gold badge" width="100" height="100">
```

Then replace `src/index.ts` with this:

```ts
import badgeUrl from '/assets/badge.svg';

const badgeImage = document.querySelector<HTMLImageElement>('#badgeImage');
if (!badgeImage) {
  throw new Error('Image #badgeImage not found');
}

badgeImage.src = badgeUrl;
console.log(badgeUrl);
```

Run `npm start`. The badge appears next to the heading. Open the browser
console with F12 and read what `badgeUrl` holds. It is not the text
`/assets/badge.svg` but a long string starting with
`data:image/svg+xml;base64,`.

## What an asset import gives you {#sec-toolchain-assets-import}

Importing a file that is not code hands your program one thing: a string the
browser can put into a `src` attribute. Vite picks that string. A small file
gets packed into the string itself, which is the `data:` address you just read.
A file over roughly four kilobytes gets copied next to your built code, and the
string becomes a path such as `/assets/rings-slS3_jD9.svg`. Your code never has
to care which one it got.

The leading slash in `'/assets/badge.svg'` means the project root, the folder
that holds `index.html` and the starter's `assets/`. A picture you keep next to
your code inside `src/` is imported with a relative path instead:

```ts
import logoUrl from './logo.svg';
```

One line in the starter lets TypeScript accept either of them. Open
`src/vite-env.d.ts`:

```ts
/// <reference types="vite/client" />
```

It pulls in Vite's type information, and part of that says an `.svg` import
gives you a string. Delete the line and the compiler answers with
`error TS2307: Cannot find module '/assets/badge.svg' or its corresponding type
declarations.` Put it back.

Only files something imports reach the finished build. A picture that lands in
`assets/` and is never mentioned stays behind.

## What npm run build produces {#sec-toolchain-assets-build}

Stop the dev server and run:

```bash
npm run build
```

```
> tsc && vite build

vite v8.2.2 building client environment for production...
transforming...
✓ 5 modules transformed.
rendering chunks...
computing gzip size...
dist/index.html                0.40 kB │ gzip: 0.28 kB
dist/assets/index-B3kKJMcG.js  1.22 kB │ gzip: 0.79 kB

✓ built in 37ms
```

A folder `dist` now sits in your project:

```
dist/
├── assets/
│   └── index-B3kKJMcG.js
└── index.html
```

No TypeScript is in there. Browsers cannot run it, so Vite translated your
program into one JavaScript file. And `dist/index.html` no longer names
`./src/index.ts`, because Vite rewrote that line to point at the built file:

```html
<script type="module" crossorigin src="/assets/index-B3kKJMcG.js"></script>
```

The letters after `index-` change whenever your code changes, and the research
box below asks what they are for. A project with a `src/styles.css` gets a
second hashed file next to it, `index-n9PMcGTe.css`.

The `build` script runs two programs, `tsc && vite build`. The type check comes
first so a program with a type error is never packaged. Vite on its own strips
the types without reading them and would build broken code without a word.

To see the result, run `npm run preview` and open `http://localhost:4173/`.
That is the finished `dist` folder, served with no dev server behind it and no
auto-reload.

Your `.gitignore` lists `dist/`, so none of this reaches git. Anybody with your
source rebuilds it in under a second.

::: {.research title="Serving a built page, and chaining two commands"}
The exercise below builds a project and opens the result, and it adds a script
that runs two programs in one line.

1. `npm run preview` starts a small web server for the `dist` folder. Why does
   double-clicking `dist/index.html` not show you the same page? Name the
   address scheme the browser uses then, and what it refuses to do with a
   `<script type="module">`.
2. The built file is named something like `index-B3kKJMcG.js`, and the letters
   change whenever your code changes. What are they for, and what would go
   wrong for a visitor who came back to the page without them?
3. A script runs `tsc --noEmit && biome check .`. What does `&&` do when `tsc`
   reports an error, and how would the script behave if it used `;` instead?

For the exam, keep the meaning of `&&` in your head. You will read npm scripts
without a search engine.
:::

## A command of your own {#sec-toolchain-assets-verify}

The `scripts` list in `package.json` takes entries of your own. Add this one,
right after `check:fix`:

```json
"verify": "tsc --noEmit && biome check ."
```

Run it:

```bash
npm run verify
```

```
> tsc --noEmit && biome check .

Checked 10 files in 3ms. No fixes applied.
```

The type check found nothing, so `&&` let Biome run, and Biome found nothing
either. From here on, `npm run verify` is what you run before every commit. A
fresh app from our template does not have the line yet, so adding it to
`package.json` is part of creating every new app from now on. The part on
testing adds the test run to that same line.

Biome reads your `.svg` files too, and it insists that a drawing says what it
shows. The `role="img"` and `aria-label` on the badge are why the run above
stayed quiet. Leave them off and you get
`lint/a11y/noSvgWithoutTitle: Alternative text title element cannot be empty`.

## House rules the agent reads {#sec-toolchain-assets-agents}

Your coding buddy carries the rules of this course, and you can give it rules
for one project on top of those. A file named `AGENTS.md` in the project root
is what agents read before they start working. Plain Markdown, short, written
for a colleague who joined today.

The starter's `.agents/skills/` folder is the same idea for instructions you
reuse across projects: each folder in there is one skill, loaded when a task
needs it, and `skills-lock.json` records where each one came from. The starter
ships `find-docs`, which sends the agent to current documentation instead of
its memory, and a later part has you write a skill of your own.

## Exercise: get a project ready to hand in {#sec-toolchain-assets-exercise}

Open your bubble chart or your beehive game in `coursework/`, whichever you
would rather keep. For a clean start instead, create a new app from our
template inside `coursework/` and use the badge from this chapter.

1. **Give the project a picture.** Move an `.svg` file into the project's
   `assets/` folder, add an `<img>` with an id to `index.html`, and set its
   `src` from `src/index.ts` with an import, the way the experiment above did.
   Expected result: the picture shows up in the browser.

2. **Add the verify script.** Put `"verify": "tsc --noEmit && biome check ."`
   into the `scripts` list in `package.json` and run `npm run verify`. Fix
   every finding and run it again until nothing is reported. An `.svg` without
   `role="img"` and `aria-label` is one finding you may have to fix.

3. **Build it and look at the result.** Run `npm run build`, then list `dist`
   and look at every file name, hashes included. Run `npm run preview` and
   use the page at `http://localhost:4173/`. Expected result: it behaves as it
   does under `npm start`, and `git status` does not mention `dist`.

4. **Let the buddy write the README.** Start `pi` in the project and ask it:
   *Write a README.md for this project. Say what it does, how to run it, and
   what each script in package.json is for.* Then read the file line by line
   and correct it by hand. Expected result: every command in the README is one
   you have run, and nothing is claimed that the project does not do.

5. **Write the house rules.** Create `AGENTS.md` in the project root with three
   rules in your own words:

   * When a script in `package.json` changes, update `README.md` in the same
     change.
   * Run `npm run verify` before reporting that you are done, and say what it
     printed.
   * Course style: single quotes, semicolons, `querySelector<T>` with a null
     check that throws, and no classes yet.

6. **Test the rules.** Ask the buddy for one small change, for example a button
   that clears the drawing or a script `"clean"` that deletes `dist`. Expected
   result: it runs `npm run verify`, and it edits `README.md` if it touched a
   script. If it skipped one, point it at `AGENTS.md` and name the rule it
   missed.

7. **Commit.** Run `npm run verify` one last time, then `git add .` and
   `git commit` with a message in the convention you picked in the git chapter.
   Expected result: `git status` prints "nothing to commit, working tree
   clean".

::: {.callout-tip}
## You review the agent, not the other way around

`AGENTS.md` makes the agent's work easier to check, and it never makes the
check unnecessary. You read the README and decide whether it is true.
:::
